title: Significant increase in network traffic with Kubernetes 1.34.1
body:
### What happened? After migrating from Kubernetes 1.29.15 to 1.34.1, we observe via our AWS bill a significant increase in inter-regional network traffic. ### What did you expect to happen? We expected that network traffic would stay consistent with older Kubernetes clusters. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? Install older and newer multi-zone Kubernetes clusters in AWS and observe the difference in network traffic in the billing console by filtering for all `DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes` usage types. ### Anything else we need to know? These clusters are managed with kops 1.34-beta.1. I will continue to investigate. ### Kubernetes version
```console $ kubectl version Client Version: v1.34.1 Kustomize Version: v5.7.1 Server Version: v1.34.1 $ ```
### Cloud provider
AWS

title: remove BlockOwnerDeletion
body:
### What happened?

BlockOwnerDeletion in resource claims created from resource claim templates, and extended resource claims by scheduler

### What did you expect to happen?

BlockOwnerDeletion should not be in the resource claim, for the reason:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134210#discussion_r2473247867

I have a hard time recommending it ever ... it is racy in terms of GC observing the child object prior to the parent object being deleted, and only ever does anything when the parent object is foreground deleted, which is not the default and very few delete operations opt into.

If the parent object must block until the child object is deleted, then use an explicit finalizer. If it doesn't really matter, then don't bother setting BlockOwnerDeletion.

title: kubernetes 1.34: The result of kubectl get cgroupDriver from the node configz is not right.
body:
### What happened?

Issue: The result of kubectl get cgroupDriver from the node configz is not right. 

Test bed:  
containerd v2.1.4
kubelet v1.34.1

Test:
Set "SystemdCgroup = true" in containerd;   
Remove cgroupDriver from kubelet config;  

Result: 
From kubelet logs:
```
# journalctl -u kubelet -f | grep -i cgroup
... kubelet[575214]: I1002 16:39:50.418991  575214 server.go:1423] "Using cgroup driver setting received from the CRI runtime" cgroupDriver="systemd"
```
Using kubectl to get cgroupDriver from the node, the result is not right, it showed "cgroupfs" like below:
```
# kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/testnode/proxy/configz | jq '.kubeletconfig.cgroupDriver'
"cgroupfs"
```

### What did you expect to happen?

let "kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/<testnode>/proxy/configz | jq '.kubeletconfig.cgroupDriver'   "
to show right cgroupDriver name. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Test bed:  
containerd v2.1.4
kubelet v1.34.1

Test:
1. Set "SystemdCgroup = true" in containerd and restart containerd
2. Remove cgroupDriver from kubelet config and restart kubelet
3. Check the result of this command: (replace <testnode> to your node name)
"kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/<testnode>/proxy/configz | jq '.kubeletconfig.cgroupDriver'   "

`_output/local/bin` is a symlink. Is that perhaps relevant?
/assign

/sig testing release
/triage accepted
I have a suspicion that it is related to `kube::golang::place_bins` not creating the symlink because of `if [[ "${platform}" == "${host_platform}" ]]`.

Debug output confirms my hunch:
```
Not creating /home/prow/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/_output/bin, linux/386 != linux/amd64

Not creating /home/prow/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/_output/bin, windows/386 != linux/amd64
Not creating /home/prow/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/_output/bin, windows/arm64 != linux/amd64
```

That's from
```patch
diff --git a/hack/lib/golang.sh b/hack/lib/golang.sh
index afc47f63bf9..65d4d66ddf3 100755
--- a/hack/lib/golang.sh
+++ b/hack/lib/golang.sh
@@ -662,6 +662,8 @@ kube::golang::place_bins() {
       rm -f "${THIS_PLATFORM_BIN}"
       mkdir -p "$(dirname "${THIS_PLATFORM_BIN}")"
       ln -s "${KUBE_OUTPUT_BIN}/${platform}" "${THIS_PLATFORM_BIN}"
+    else
+      kube::log::info "Not creating ${THIS_PLATFORM_BIN}, ${platform} != ${host_platform}"
     fi
 
     V=3 kube::log::status "Placing binaries for ${platform} in ${KUBE_OUTPUT_BIN}/${platform}"
```

Something seems to have changed such that `KUBE_CLIENT_PLATFORMS` no longer includes linux/amd64 - but only in the CI environment. It still works for me locally.

I can reproduce this now, after `kind build node-image` which uses `build/run.sh` to build containerized, `_output/bin` will be:

```
$ ls -la _output/bin
lrwxrwxrwx 1 bentheelder primarygroup 60 Oct 15 17:14 _output/bin -> /go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/_output/dockerized/bin/linux/amd64
```

That's the right path *in the container* but not for the host.

IIRC relative symlinks are possible, and that's probably the cleanest solution.

Working on a patch.
That makes more sense. My previous log output was incomplete, it didn't show that the symlink was created, only for which platforms it wasn't created.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134628 should do it

So on 1.34, if you build "local" first:
```console
make clean
make WHAT=ginkgo
```

Then build something "dockerized":
```console
build/run.sh make WHAT=test/e2e/e2e.test
```

It will actually keep `_output/bin` pointed at an (absolute) symlink to the "local" platform specific output directory ~~and copy in the "dockerized" binaries.~~

~~So the "local" output actually becomes converged ... this behavior seems odd but we should preserve it to avoid breakage.~~

~~It also depends on the order after `make clean` removes `_output`, if you do only dockerized builds then `_output/bin` will not be created on `release-1.34`.~~

~~But if you build _any_ binary non-dockerized first, we will create `_output/bin` pointing at the "local" output directory and then subsequent "dockerized" builds will copy the binaries from the dockerized output to the local output directory.~~

So we should unbreak the DRA job, but depending on `_output/bin` behavior is pretty fragile, and we should consider using the specific dockerized / local paths or `kube::util::find-binary`.

Tested @ 00b6a4c7afd

Testing some more and being pretty careful to `make clean` between iterations, I think the "correct" behavior from 1.34 is to only ever populate `_output/bin` as a symlink to `_output/local/bin/$HOST_PLATFORM` and that will only contain those "local" binaries, never "dockerized".

That behavior doesn't feel terribly helpful, but it appears to have been ~stable for ~10 years so let's try to keep it ...

> Something seems to have changed such that KUBE_CLIENT_PLATFORMS no longer includes linux/amd64 - but only in the CI environment. It still works for me locally.

This is a red-herring, your test uses an "else" on when it does find that platform (since linux/amd64 is the host) so this is expected.

But what's not expected is that `_output/bin` will ever be pointing at the dockerized binaries, apparently (which in this case have the kind node binaries, but not ginkgo and e2e.test).

That's doubly broken on master because the absolute paths are wrong when generated from the container.

On 1.34 we will create `bin -> /go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/_output/dockerized/bin/linux/arm64` but only inside the container, which will not by rsynced out.

It will however persist on subsequent usage of the build container:

```console

+++ [1015 15:51:19] Output from this container will NOT be rsynced out upon completion. Set KUBE_RUN_COPY_OUTPUT=y to enable.

total 16
drwxr-xr-x  3 484827 89939 4096 Oct 15 15:48 .
drwxr-xr-x 22 484827 89939 4096 Oct 15 15:44 ..
lrwxrwxrwx  1 484827 89939   60 Oct 15 15:48 bin -> /go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/_output/dockerized/bin/linux/arm64
drwxr-xr-x  4 484827 89939 4096 Oct 15 15:45 dockerized

$ ls -la _output
total 0
drwxr-xr-x@  4 bentheelder  primarygroup   128 Oct 15 15:48 .
drwxr-xr-x@ 42 bentheelder  primarygroup  1344 Oct 15 15:44 ..
drwxr-xr-x@  4 bentheelder  primarygroup   128 Oct 15 15:45 dockerized
drwxr-xr-x@  3 bentheelder  primarygroup    96 Oct 15 15:43 images

I think https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134632 may be a ~reasonable compatibility fix, it builds on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134628 which we should do regardless.

title: DRA: plugin can not pass a mount for a pod with hostUsers: false
body:
### What happened?

When a pod has  `hostUsers: false` in spec, then all mounts should have `UidMappings` and `GidMappings`. In Kubelet this is done in [applyPlatformSpecificContainerConfig](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container_linux.go#L72) function. However, in DRA plugin we do not know about a user namespace generated for a pod in [UserNSManager](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/userns/userns_manager.go#L393). Also, in [CDI](https://github.com/cncf-tags/container-device-interface/blob/main/specs-go/config.go#L49) we can not specify the `UidMappings` and `GidMappings`.  So, in container we will have a permission denied error (if mount won't have a 0666 permissions).

```bash
vboxuser@vboxuser:~/dra-plugin-health-example$ kubectl  exec -ti example-pod -- /bin/bash
Defaulted container "container1" out of: container1, container2, container3
root@example-pod:/# ls -la /opt/exampmle-dir/  
ls: cannot open directory '/opt/exampmle-dir/': Permission denied
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Do not have a Permission Denied error.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The example DRA [plugin](https://github.com/everzakov/dra-plugin-health-example/tree/userns-with-mounts) with passing a mount as CDI device.

    image: docker.io/library/ubuntu:22.04
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    command: ["sleep", "2000"]
    resources:
      claims:
      - name: claim-templtate

```

title: APF significantly under-reporting seats for watches without RV
body: From a recent study, we observed API server’s CPU usage (on a 96 vCPU instance) vs "current_executing_seats" was extremely skewed: Computing the CPU usage/seat during that time, it swings quite a bit (0.4-2.0): For that period in the middle where CPU usage/seat is relatively high, majority of the seat usage comes from "workload-low" priority level: Dissecting it further, we can correlate the usage to watch calls from a particular client: These were all watches with RV unset (could've also been RV set to 0): Such calls are expensive upfront due to initial "Add" events being generated for the entire collection, as required by our [API semantics](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#semantics-for-watch). **So why do they have such low seat usage?** The API server's seat calculation logic intends to count watch calls that don't need to send init events at the lowest cost. It does this by checking SendInitialEvents parameter isn't set to true ([xref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0f8471a6f5b00e93409422f1a39e4655651c105a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/flowcontrol/request/list_work_estimator.go#L91-L95)). But that misses the RV unset/0 cases (i.e. legacy watches), under reporting their penalty too. We need to exclude those from incorrectly being assigned minimum seats. **What's the problem with low seat usage?** APF doesn't provide enough protection to CPU usage (as seen above) if a barrage of such legacy watch requests strike the API server. /sig api-machinery /kind bug cc @MikeSpreitzer @wojtek-t @serathius - I can send out a fix for this if no objections.

title: kubectl events --for does not show events where involvedObject.apiVersion is missing
body:
### What happened?

When running `kubectl events --for Node/<node-name>`, some events (such as OOMKilling events from kernel-monitor node-problem-detector) do not appear, even though they are visible in `kubectl get events`. Upon investigation, these missing events have an `involvedObject` without an `apiVersion` field.

Example:

This event is **not** shown by `kubectl events --for Node/<node-name>`:

```yaml
kind: Event
count: 1074
eventTime: null
firstTimestamp: "2025-10-07T22:00:52Z"
involvedObject:
  kind: Node
  name: XXXXXXXXXX
  uid: XXXXXXXXXX
# apiVersion is missing
message: ...
reason: OOMKilling
source:
  component: kernel-monitor
```

But this event **is** shown:
```yaml
kind: Event
count: 11
eventTime: null
firstTimestamp: "2025-10-09T01:19:49Z"
involvedObject:
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Node
  name: XXXXXXXXXX
  uid: df71ea00-f008-41b2-bb6e-a21466b7bf38
# apiVersion is present
message: ...
reason: DisruptionBlocked
source:
  component: karpenter
```

The relevant code in `kubectl events` sets a field selector:
```go
listOptions.FieldSelector = fields.AndSelectors(
    fields.OneTermEqualSelector("involvedObject.kind", o.forGVK.Kind),
    fields.OneTermEqualSelector("involvedObject.apiVersion", o.forGVK.GroupVersion().String()),
    fields.OneTermEqualSelector("involvedObject.name", o.forName)).String()
```
Events missing `involvedObject.apiVersion` are excluded from the results.

### What did you expect to happen?

Events for the specified Node should be shown even if their `involvedObject.apiVersion` field is missing, as long as `kind` and `name` match.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Install node-problem-detector in the cluster
2. Generate a node event with OOMKilling (e.g., run a memory-hogging process on a node).
3. Ensure an event is created that is visible in `kubectl get events` but missing `involvedObject.apiVersion`.
4. Run `kubectl events --for Node/<node-name>`
5. Observe that the event does not appear, but it does with `kubectl get events`.

### Anything else we need to know?

This bug can be worked around by omitting `--for`, but that makes filtering by object impossible. The filtering logic should be more tolerant to missing fields.

nodes.title: Use lock-free for unguarded isHidden/isDeprecated fields
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Fixes https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134372

Access to the isHidden / isDeprecated fields was not guarded, and is in the hot path from metrics usage.

Switching to lock-free booleans.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
<!--
If no, just write "NONE" in the release-note block below.
If yes, a release note is required:
Enter your extended release note in the block below. If the PR requires additional action from users switching to the new release, include the string "action required".

For more information on release notes see: https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/guide/release-notes.md
-->
```release-note
Fixes a possible data race during metrics registration
```

/sig instrumentation
/cc @richabanker @pohly

title: Node swap metric uses memory timestamp instead of swap timestamp
body:
### What happened?

The `collectNodeSwapMetrics` function emits node swap usage metrics with the timestamp from node memory stats rather than swap stats. This issue was caught in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132945

### What did you expect to happen?

Node swap usage metrics should use the swap stat timestamp to accurately reflect the time of stat collection, matching the handling for pod and container swap metrics.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Review `collectNodeSwapMetrics` in `pkg/kubelet/metrics/collectors/resource_metrics.go`.

### Anything else we need to know?

Pod and container swap metrics already use the correct swap stat timestamp.

title: API Server returns panic message to caller when Creating CronJob with Some Invalid Schedule Format
body:
### What happened?

API Server panics when creating a CronJob with an invalid schedule format like `"TZ=0"`. This causes a slice bounds out of range error in the robfig/cron parser.


### What did you expect to happen?

API Server should return a proper validation error instead of panic.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?


1. Create a CronJob YAML with invalid schedule:
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: daily-backup
spec:
  schedule: "TZ=0"  # Invalid: missing space and cron expression
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: backup
            image: alpine
            command: ["/bin/sh"]
            args: ["-c", "echo 'Starting backup...' && date"]
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

2. Apply the YAML:
```bash
kubectl apply -f test-cron-job.yaml
```

**Actual behavior:**
The API server panics with:

/assign
/sig api-machinery
/sig apps
/assign

HI @PersistentJZH, im a new contributor and assigned myself to the issue you were already assigned without knowing it would affect you.

Sorry for the unassignment! Ill remove my assignement here.
/unassign
/assign
Let's see if we can get https://github.com/robfig/cron/pull/555 landed, given that there hasn't been much activity in that library for a while. If not, I'm fine addressing this problem on our side.
/triage accepted
Just for clarity, the API server doesn't *exit* on the panic, right? (it is recovered and handled for the particular request)

> Just for clarity, the API server doesn't _exit_ on the panic, right? (it is recovered and handled for the particular request)

Yes, apiserver will not exit on the panic, and will be recovered through runtime.HandleCrash.

### What happened?

title: resp.Body not closed in transformResponse in client-go may cause memory leak
body:
### What happened? In staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/request.go, within the transformResponse function, the HTTP response body (resp.Body) is read using io.ReadAll, but is not explicitly closed afterward. According to Go best practices, failing to close the response body can lead to resource leaks, particularly file descriptors or sockets, over time or under high load. This has the potential to degrade performance or cause failures in API clients using client-go. Reference: https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/master/rest/request.go#L1177 ### What did you expect to happen? I expected resp.Body to be closed after reading its contents, following Go best practices for HTTP response handling, to ensure network resources are properly released. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? - Use a client-go-based controller or CLI that makes repeated API requests to the Kubernetes API server. - Monitor file descriptor usage or open sockets on the client process. - Observe that over time, these resources are not released as expected, indicating a leak. ### Anything else we need to know? - The fix is to add defer resp.Body.Close() immediately after confirming resp.Body != nil and before reading the body. - See Go’s [http.Response documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#Response) for details on why response bodies must be closed. - This issue can lead to resource exhaustion on long-running controllers or high-traffic clients. ### Kubernetes version Affected in all recent versions using current client-go (e.g., v0.33.x, v0.34.x) ### Cloud provider
AWS

```console # On Linux: $ cat /etc/os-release # paste output here $ uname -a # paste output here # On Windows: C:\> wmic os get Caption, Version, BuildNumber, OSArchitecture # paste output here ```

title: Preemption process does not leave a trait in the scheduler cache causing a race
body:
### What happened?

The preemption process that is initiated by the scheduler does not leave the immediate trait in the cache. Due to a race, a pod may come back to the scheduling queue before the in-memory state gets updated (receives a notification about a pod being deleted or marked for deletion DeletionTimestamp != nil) and start the same preemption process again.

Whenever the preemption process identifies a pod eligible for preemption, but learns the pod does no longer exist, it immediately puts the preemptor back to scheduling queue (since it may never receive a notification that wakes it up from the unschedulable queue) and the process repeats in a tight loop, each time producing a pod delete api call.

The factor that triggers this issue is the fact that when a pod being preempted is in the binding process, the scheduler lets it finish the process and IGNORES pod delete notifications, waiting for this async binding process to fail. This creates quite a wide window making the problem very likely to happen in a specific use case, like autoscaling when initial pods jump into nodes they were not intended to and need to be preempted right after). Large number of outgoing api-calls (to delete non-existing pod) generates a big load on the api-server and may generate a snowball effect.

The issue itself exists from a long time, but the PR which closed the loop by activating preemptor pod on failure was added to 1.34 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/133213

### What did you expect to happen?

The information about a non-existing pod should be reflected in the in-memory cache to cut that loop.

It could be either recorded right after pod delete was accepted or even better whenever any attempt to delete it failed (non-existing pod)

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We haven't managed to reproduce it in isolation

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

When pod is in the binding phase it occupies the space on the node (is assumed). When the higher priority pod tried to preempt such pod, it deleted it from the cluster, but it remained in the scheduler's cache. Since the binding phase can take some time (PreBind, Bind), the pod occupies the space for a long time. The higher priority pod, when retried, would try to preempt the pod again, wasting scheduling cycles and API calls to the kube-apiserver.

In some scenarios, this behavior can seriously affect the scheduling performance, by continuously preempting the already deleted pod.

This PR forgets the pod from a cache when the pod delete event is registered by the scheduler. Such pod will eventually fail its binding cycle as previously, but the space won't be occupied anymore. Similar behavior is implemented for pods that are under graceful termination.

title: [kubelet] time shift and `failed to reserve container name`
body:
### What happened?

After a liveness failure the kubelet tried to restart the container `test-container`. The node clock stepped backwards about 40 seconds at the same moment. Because `podWorkerLoop` calls `podCache.GetNewerThan(podUID, lastSyncTime)`, the cached pod status never looked newer than the saved `lastSyncTime`. The kubelet kept the old `RestartCount`, called `CreateContainer` again with attempt `1`, and containerd returned:

```
failed to reserve container name "test-container_test-container-68b789996c-q9kxh_d8-cloud-instance-manager_fe9ba7d1-5308-44ef-a81c-83133bf88c50_1": name ... is reserved for "d553f9f992855e898c29b05b6487da56580ab760db155bfd90da20e8fe8a98bc"
```

### What did you expect to happen?


Even if the node clock jumps backwards, kubelet should notice that the previous container already exists and should wait for a fresh pod status before calling `CreateContainer` again. The restart attempt should be `2`, not `1`, so containerd does not reject the request

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Run Kubernetes v1.31.10 with containerd on a test node.
2. Deploy any pod that continuously crashes (e.g. fails liveness probe so it loops in `CrashLoopBackOff`).
3. On the same node run:

```bash
while true
do
     sudo date -s "+10 minutes"
     sleep 1
     sudo date -s "-10 minutes"
     sleep 1
done
 ```

4. Watch kubelet and containerd logs. After several restarts you will see kubelet making a second `CreateContainer` call with attempt `1`, followed by containerd logging `failed to reserve container name`.

### Anything else we need to know?

```
I0918 16:09:49.994636     550 kuberuntime_container.go:808] "Killing container with a grace period" pod="d8-cloud-instance-manager/bashible-apiserver-68b789996c-q9kxh" containerID="containerd://c42fbc64c45cd657eeaceee5c2326f3e64057d551d9340629670487c0247e0c5"
E0918 16:08:41.636161     550 log.go:32] "CreateContainer in sandbox from runtime service failed" err="rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to reserve container name ..."
```

title: DRA consumable capacity failed to allocate the same device once device consumes counterSet
body:
### What happened?

The device that consumed counterSet is skipped if the counter is not left enough even it was selected and allowMultipleAllocations is set.

The reason is that the checkAvailableCounters is called and return false as it is selected once before the capacity will be checked.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/69aca29e6def5873779cbd392bd9a1bad124c586/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go#L1209


### What did you expect to happen?

The device which is once consumed capacity from the counterSet should be able to allocated if there is enough capacity left for another request.  Meaning that the alloc.checkAvailableCounters should be skipped - do not check, do not consume.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

counterSet0: 4
device1 (allowMultipleAllocations): consume 3 from counterSet0
device2 (allowMultipleAllocations): consume 4 from counterSet0

req0: request capacity 1
req1: request capacity 1

req0 can get device 1 but req1 is failed to get the same device

title: AssumeCache may detect the PersistentVolume update later than the scheduler's event handlers
body:
### What happened?

Let's say we have a scenario where Pod is rejected waiting for a PersistentVolume to be available.
When the PersistentVolume status is updated to `Available`, the scheduler is notified via event handlers.

One of such handlers, in [eventhandling.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/18c188467d8ae00042b61f82aa159094336b657e/pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go#L566) is responsible for triggering the Pod's scheduling retry. In this case, the reason is valid, so the Pod is placed in the activeQ (or backoffQ) and then taken to the scheduling.

However, during the (pre)filtering of VolumeBinding plugin, the PersistentVolume objects are [listed](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/18c188467d8ae00042b61f82aa159094336b657e/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumebinding/binder.go#L825) from the plugin's AssumeCache, which have its own set of the [event handlers](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/18c188467d8ae00042b61f82aa159094336b657e/pkg/scheduler/util/assumecache/assume_cache.go#L208-L214). If these handlers receive the PV update event later than the main scheduler's handlers, VolumeBinding takes the decision based on an old data, e.g. a PersistentVolume with an old state. As a result, the Pod is [rejected](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/18c188467d8ae00042b61f82aa159094336b657e/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumebinding/binder.go#L885) and goes back to the scheduling queue.

Ultimately, there won't be any event that would wake up such Pod again, so it will wait indefinitely (precisely, it will be retried by the flushing mechanism that we would like to eventually remove).

This behavior causes the `volumescheduling` integration test to flake: https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-release-master-blocking#integration-master

/sig scheduling
/sig storage
/kind flake

### What did you expect to happen?

VolumeBinding should have a consistent view of PersistentVolumes with the main scheduler's event handlers.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run the integration tests with low parallelism:
```sh
KUBE_INTEGRATION_TEST_MAX_CONCURRENCY=2 make test-integration WHAT="test/integration/volumescheduling" KUBE_TEST_ARGS="-run TestVolumeBindingRescheduling"
```

The fix for this should be what I did for DRA: react to events provided by the assume cache instead of the underlying informer. That functionality didn't exist in the assume cache when it was added for volumes, but it is there now for exactly this purpose.

<!--

/kind feature

Optionally add one or more of the following kinds if applicable:
/kind api-change
/kind deprecation
/kind failing-test
/kind flake
/kind regression
-->

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Currently volume and dynamic-resource plugin shares an AssumeCache implementation. However, they features significantly different use case.  DRA call Assume() on objects returned by APIServer, but volume call Assume() on objects yet to be sent to the APIServer.

VolumeBinding plugin only makes one update request, while DynamicResource makes 2 requests (add finalizer then update allocation status).  Taking advantage of this, currently the volume cache is simpler:

1. Reserve: assume PV/PVC will be updated
2. PreBind: really send the update request
3. AssumeCache receives an update from informer and overwrite the assumed state.
   - if PreBind succeeded, this will surely include the update from step 2.
   - if PreBind is not finished yet, and this is an irrelevant update, it is safe to overwrite the assumed state, because our update in PreBind will surely fail with Conflict.

While for DynamicResource:

1. Reserve: add devices to inFlightAllocations
2. PreBind:
   1. send the 2 update requests
   2. add the returned object into AssumeCache
   3. AssumeCache dispatch events synchronously to update allocatedDevices
   4. remove devices from inFlightAllocations

DynamicResource needs some features from AssumeCache that is not necessary for VolumeBinding:
1. DynamicResource needs strictly ordered update events to update allocatedDevices, including those from Assume() and Restore()
2. DynamicResource needs to compare ResourceVersion to prevent the assumed state from being overwritten by older version from informer.  While this works, the [doc][1] says: "you must not compare resource versions for greater-than or less-than relationships".

Given so much difference, it can be beneficial to fork another simpler AssumeCache for VolumeBinding plugin. Because of no need to send events, the lite AssumeCache is a passive component. It only record the assumed version without copying all objects from informer into its local cache. When reading, we read from both informer and local cache.  So it will always be up-to-date with informer, no need to wait for event handler.

This resolves a race condition where AssumeCache and scheduler queue both receive events from informer. When a pod is scheduling due to PV update event, the PVCache may be not updated yet because it has not processed the relevant event.

The lite version still listens events from informer, but only for cleaning up its local cache to save memory.

[1]: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#resource-versions

title: kube-proxy config option --iptables-sync-period only works in specific cases
body:
### What happened?

Hello, Regarding the **kube-proxy** `--iptables-sync-period` config option. The official description says:

```
An interval (e.g. '5s', '1m', '2h22m') indicating how frequently various re-synchronizing and cleanup operations are performed. Must be greater than 0.
```

However, the actual sync occurs every 1 hour. 
https://sourcegraph.com/github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes@release-1.25/-/blob/pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go?L326

Additionally, it appears that the sync doesn't occur even if the NAT table is flushed. 
Outside the changes to the Endpoints resources when the re-sync is expected, the only other case where the re-sync will occur is when **KUBE-PROXY-CHAIN** is modified/deleted in the `mangle` table.
https://sourcegraph.com/github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes@release-1.25/-/blob/pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go?L328

I think the description should be updated to reflect this if this is the expected behavior.

### What did you expect to happen?

The description of `--iptables-sync-period` should clearly mention when the re-synchronization occurs.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Flush iptables `nat` table
- `kube-proxy` doesn't re-sync the iptables rules within the defined `--iptables-sync-period`

 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/be361a18dda0f2fab1f5e25f8067a9ed43fc3b89/pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go#L313

We should probably update the docs to clarify that 1h is the maximum. 

Were you attempting to sync less frequently than 1h? For what purpose?

Thanks for responding @BenTheElder. We have a distributed firewall mechanism that works alongside of kube-proxy. There are a few scenarios where the iptables can be flushed and 1hr wait time to recover isn't feasible for our environment.

I see the till v1.32 the behavior is same, the latest code you shared appears to be applicable from v1.34 ref #131615.

(Looks like the issue is very similar to #129128, linking here in case any wants to get more context.)

> There are a few scenarios where the iptables can be flushed and 1hr wait time to recover isn't feasible for our environment.

Right, so you're *not* trying to use >1h then right?

You can set a lower interval, and the default is 30s (sync period) / 1s (min)
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d5065bdf192b2ebb723657b3432c66ce3ea15b23/pkg/proxy/apis/config/v1alpha1/defaults.go#L62-L67

It's possible there was some confusion/overriding between config and flags?

---

EDIT: Clearly the flag info should be corrected to not suggest a value greater than the maximum, and to document the maximum.
@danwinship is the expert of this area

>Right, so you're not trying to use >1h then right?
No, we actually want it to sync at a specified `--iptables-sync-period`.

Based on the below code (<= v1.32), it only does sync at a 1 hour and doesn't honor `--iptables-sync-period`. You can check the below function call that handles the sync.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.32/pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go#L328

> ```
> An interval (e.g. '5s', '1m', '2h22m') indicating how frequently various re-synchronizing and cleanup operations are performed. Must be greater than 0.
> ```
> 
> However, the actual sync occurs every 1 hour.

The docs say that it controls "various re-synchronizing and cleanup operations". It doesn't say it controls every possible resync. (The docs are vague about exactly what it does, because it doesn't really do anything super useful any more, because the code doesn't work the same way it did when that option was added.)

> We have a distributed firewall mechanism that works alongside of kube-proxy. There are a few scenarios where the iptables can be flushed and 1hr wait time to recover isn't feasible for our environment.

kube-proxy assumes that when firewalls flush the iptables rules, they will flush _all_ iptables rules in all tables (because that's how all of the standard distro firewall services work). If you have your own firewall system and you need to flush iptables, you should do something like:

```sh
for table in filter nat raw mangle; do
    iptables -t ${table} -F
    iptables -t ${table} -X
done
```

And kube-proxy will notice that and recover. (kube-proxy has to poll `mangle` rather than `nat` because iptables is terrible, and polling `nat` regularly would slow kube-proxy syncing down by creating contention for the iptables lock.)

(This isn't documented because that's the way all firewall systems we were aware of already worked, so there didn't really seem to be any need to document it.)

(And FTR, one of the things `--iptables-sync-period` controls is how often it polls to see if its canary chains have been deleted, so if the default 30s is too high, you can change that. Though, in that case, you should really try to make it so your firewall doesn't need to flush kube-proxy's rules...)

body:
### What happened?

During testing of the consumable capacity feature using dra-example-driver, I encountered several issues affecting allocation and scheduling behavior. 

One issue is about missing share ID in CDI pb. I believe that it can add for beta criteria updates since there are some workaround can be done at driver side (i.e., append device name with share id).

A more critical issue is in the scheduler’s device allocation logic. When one of the requested devices has already been allocated by another claim, the scheduler fails to proceed with allocating the remaining devices. This is due to a bug in the CmpRequestOverCapacity call within the allocateDevice function. This behavior was not covered by existing tests, and it's also relevant to the wrong test case for AllocationMode: All.

### What did you expect to happen?

Should pass the following test case:

			},

title: Kubelet Volume Manager can erroneously mark volume as unmounted.
body:
### What happened?

We observed an edge case where an API server transient issue can cause a volume to be marked as unmounted in the volume manager's ASW, and making the subsequent `NodeVolumeUnstage` calls to fail due to dangling publish mounts.

The sequence of events is:
1. A map volume operation is kicked off.
2. The API server has a transient issue, causing the map volume operation to fail with `Error: MapVolume.MarkVolumeAsMounted failed while expanding volume for volume $PVC`. This error happens after the `MapPodDevice` (and therefore the `NodePublishVolume`) call has already succeeded. This causes the volume mount to be marked as uncertain and the map to be requeued.
3. When the operation retries,  the api server issue causes the MapPodDevice to fail with `blockMapper.publishVolumeForBlock failed to get NodePublishSecretRef`
4. This error causes `markVolumeErrorState` to be called. The logic here[0] falls into a branch that marks the volume as unmounted in ASW, since the mount is marked uncertain.
5. At this point the pod is deleted, so the map operation doesn't happen again. Since the volume is marked unmounted, the VM reconciler doesn't call unpublish for this pod and volume pair.

[0] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/56dd5ab10ff19aa9ebe438122a00472c4135de23/pkg/volume/util/operationexecutor/operation_generator.go#L819


### What did you expect to happen?

All volumes are unpublished correctly after the pod is deleted.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Once `MapPodDevice` completes, trigger pod deletion and inject API failures. This should cause the pod to be deleted without unpublish being called.

### Anything else we need to know?

/priority important-soon
We really expect the tests to leave the cluster in a clean state and be safe to run repeatedly for development.

A test in the default suite should not be doing that, it makes me think we might need to mark even the remaining test as [Disruptive].

End-users also sometimes run these tests to validate their clusters. At least _most_ of them focus on `[Conformance]` thankfully.

I think it is a known issue that extended resources remain forever in a node status, even after uninstalling the corresponding Device Plugin. cc @klueska for conformation.

However, they should be reported with zero capacity. The production code needs to handle that situation gracefully. Does it currently assume `example.com/foo is set == resources provided by device plugin`? I think that assumption is false, it needs to check for `example.com/foo > 0`.

Node status after removing the example device plugin:
```
    allocatable:
      cpu: "36"
      ephemeral-storage: 1055762868Ki
      example.com/resource: "0"
      hugepages-1Gi: "0"
      hugepages-2Mi: "0"
      memory: 65531360Ki
      pods: "110"
    capacity:
      cpu: "36"
      ephemeral-storage: 1055762868Ki
      example.com/resource: "2"
      hugepages-1Gi: "0"
      hugepages-2Mi: "0"
      memory: 65531360Ki
      pods: "110"
```

> [deployDevicePlugin](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/790393ae92e97262827d4f1fba24e8ae65bbada0/test/e2e/dra/deploy_device_plugin.go#L34) leaks the extended resource example.com/resource in node's status.Allocatable/Capacity. This causes conflicts for multiple tests using the extended resource in the same cluster.

This goes beyond test conflicts. Suppose a node was using a Device Plugin for some hardware. The admin uninstalls the Device Plugin and installs the DRA driver instead. Now the extended resources must be allocated via the DRA driver, no matter what the node status says. This is a blocker for beta.

/priority important-soon
/milestone v1.35

if kubelet keeps the extended resources from uninstalled device plugin in node.status.Allocatable: 0, then admin should restart the kubelet to clear it. It is confusing to see an extended resource is scheduled to a node with node.status.Allocatable: 0.

> Node status after removing the example device plugin:
> 
> ```
>     allocatable:
>       cpu: "36"
>       ephemeral-storage: 1055762868Ki
>       example.com/resource: "0"
>       hugepages-1Gi: "0"
>       hugepages-2Mi: "0"
>       memory: 65531360Ki
>       pods: "110"
>     capacity:
>       cpu: "36"
>       ephemeral-storage: 1055762868Ki
>       example.com/resource: "2"
>       hugepages-1Gi: "0"
>       hugepages-2Mi: "0"
>       memory: 65531360Ki
>       pods: "110"
> ```

@swatisehgal @ffromani Just wondering why this is done this way? Would it help if we  stop counting unhealthy devices for capacity [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.34/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L473)?

> if kubelet keeps the extended resources from uninstalled device plugin in node.status.Allocatable: 0, then admin should restart the kubelet to clear it.

Is that known to clear it?

> It is confusing to see an extended resource is scheduled to a node with node.status.Allocatable: 0.

Have you seen that happening? It seems that the scheduler doesn't schedule pods onto such nodes.

> I suspect it's implemented this way in purpose to distinguish between local node resources and cluster-level resources.

I'm not sure about that. That node status isn't about cluster-level resources. I suspect it is more because the kubelet cannot distinguish between "device plugin temporarily down" and "permanently removed".

> I'm not sure about that. That node status isn't about cluster-level resources. 

This is what I've read [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.34/pkg/kubelet/nodestatus/setters.go#L278-L280). 

> I suspect it is more because the kubelet cannot distinguish between "device plugin temporarily down" and "permanently removed".

It's not that sophisticated, at least to my knowledge. When plugin deregistered or disconnected, Kubelet sets all its devices as `Unhealthy`, but includes them into the node status' `Capacity`. This is what you've quoted above: `Capacity: 2` in your example are those `Unhealthy` devices. This is why [I've asked maintainers about it](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133488#issuecomment-3213349044).

Good news is that the API server doesn't seem to be involved in updating `Capacity` and `Allocatable` fields. They're maintained by Kubelet. At least this is what I see in my experiments.

> > if kubelet keeps the extended resources from uninstalled device plugin in node.status.Allocatable: 0, then admin should restart the kubelet to clear it.
> 
> Is that known to clear it?
> 
node.status.Allocatable/Capacity is owned by kubelet, hence i think so, though i have not verified it. @bart0sh did you have a chance to verify it?

> > It is confusing to see an extended resource is scheduled to a node with node.status.Allocatable: 0.
> 
> Have you seen that happening? It seems that the scheduler doesn't schedule pods onto such nodes.
> 
scheduler could potentially schedule pods onto such nodes if those nodes happen to have DRA extended resources, and we change the DRA extended resources logic to allow that.

@yliaog 
> node.status.Allocatable/Capacity is owned by kubelet, hence i think so, though i have not verified it. @bart0sh did you have a chance to verify it?

So far I've changed Kubelet code to set both fields to 0 when plugin is unregistered and they stay unchanged for a long time. After that I went further - changed the code to stop publishing those fields if they're set to 0 and they've disappeared from the node status. That worked well.

However, I suspect that it was a design decision to publish them and also count Unhealthy devices as capacity to make them visible. For example if Allocatable is set to 0 and Capacity to 2, educated user/admin would understand that there are 2 unhealthy devices on the node and most probably it means that device plugin is disconnected. 
But all of this is just an educated guess. @klueska @ffromani and @swatisehgal can explain how it was designed and how it works.

@yliaog No, it was not a design decision. [Device Plugin KEP](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/3573-device-plugin) explicitly states that 
```
In general we expect Kubelet to remove any devices that are owned by
the failed device plugin from the node capacity.
We also expect node allocatable to be equal to node capacity.
```
which is good for us as we can consider current Kubelet behaviour as a bug and fix it.

> [@pohly](https://github.com/pohly) [@yliaog](https://github.com/yliaog)
> 
> > [@pohly](https://github.com/pohly) commented [4 days ago](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133488#issuecomment-3197978535)
> > I think it is a known issue that extended resources remain forever in a node status, even after uninstalling the corresponding Device Plugin. cc [@klueska](https://github.com/klueska) for conformation.
> 
> I tried to modify Kubelet not to report local node extended resources with Allocatable/Capacity 0 and it worked just fine. However, I suspect it's implemented this way in purpose to distinguish between local node resources and cluster-level resources. [@ffromani](https://github.com/ffromani) [@swatisehgal](https://github.com/swatisehgal) [@SergeyKanzhelev](https://github.com/SergeyKanzhelev) Is it correct assumption?

I can only quickly comment before I'm going OOO for the full next week (till Sep 1).
This is likely correct, and there is no clear decisive record of why it is implemented like that. To be reasonnably sure, we need to reconstruct history from comments (both design docs at time) and reviews. Is not unheard that a [very early implementation bug survived till today,](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/119423#issuecomment-2934790530) and I won't be surprised if we find more instances along the way.

Another main problem is this behavior has been with us since many years. It's very likely someone depends on it in a way we can't imagine (Hyrum's law in full swing). So, albeit I stress that the suggested behavior looks better from every angle we can think of, we need to be super careful about the fix.

I think we need to carefully address these 2 items before we can move on.
And, to be redundant: I agree and I like much more if kubelet clears the extended resources as proposed.

@ffromani Thank you for the detailed answer! To trigger the discussion I've submitted https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/133727, so we can discuss it further. The change is simple, but I agree that we need to be careful with it due to the reasons you've explained.
@yliaog While we're discussing the fix (which can take long, I suspect), can you give us more details about the issues the current behaviour creates for the extended resources support for DRA?

> if kubelet keeps the extended resources from uninstalled device plugin in node.status.Allocatable: 0, then admin should restart the kubelet to clear it.

@klueska said that restarting the kubelet does *not* clear the status.

> can you give us more details about the issues the current behaviour creates for the extended resources support for DRA?

I [believe](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133488#issuecomment-3204285168) updating a node from device plugin to DRA does not work unless the admin also manually fixes the status.

I agree that fixing kubelet is going to take time. Even if gets fixed, due to version skew clusters might use an older kubelet without the change. We should also look into fixing this in the scheduler. I think it should be safe to try with DRA when `allocatable` is zero: if the scheduler was trying to schedule without DRA, it would simply fail. With DRA there is at least a chance that it works.
/retitle DRA Extended Resource: support nodes where device plugin was uninstalled

> I think it should be safe to try with DRA when allocatable is zero

zero capacity and zero allocatable even safer. It means that plugin either unregistered or disconnected **at least** [5 minutes ago](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.34/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/types.go#L116-L120).

> I https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133488#issuecomment-3204285168 updating a node from device plugin to DRA does not work unless the admin also manually fixes the status.

I'm guessing here, but stopping Kubelet, removing its checkpoint file and starting it again should do the trick as well.

> zero capacity and zero allocatable even safer.

Safer in which sense? What problem does waiting for 5 minutes avoid?

If `allocatable` dropped to zero only because the device driver temporarily got stopped (e.g. for an update), then it's still safe to try scheduling with DRA because there won't be DRA devices for the node, because those are still owned by the device driver.

> Safer in which sense?

In a sense that there are more chances that the scheduled workload will be successfully executed on the node. We don't support running both DRA and DP on the same node, do we?

> In a sense that there are more chances that the scheduled workload will be successfully executed on the node.

I think it's the other way around. If `allocatable` is zero, scheduling is guaranteed to fail unless we try to use DRA. Trying with DRA immediately *increases* the chances that scheduling will succeed. Waiting for `capacity` to become zero is *reducing* the chances.

> We don't support running both DRA and DP on the same node, do we?

Not for the same hardware.

> i see is it may cause application operators confusion, they see their pods are scheduled to a node with allocatable == 0.

But only if the DRA driver has been installed, right? Why would this be confusing? The admin clearly wants to manage the hardware with DRA, so scheduling the pod is what they want.

nodes.title: Treat extended resources as inactive when allocatable is 0
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This change updates scheduler and kubelet logic to treat device plugin resources with zero healthy devices(NodeStatus.Allocatable: 0) as inactive when the DRAExtendedResource feature is enabled. When a device plugin is disconnected or uninstalled, the resource is no longer considered a device plugin resource and can be processed by a DRA driver.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes: #133488

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

When device plugin is uninstalled, Kubelet keeps updating node status with the information about its resources, which makes current implementation of the DRA support for extended resources to consider those resources as mainained by
the device plugin. This PR changes this behaviour by allowing scheduling workloads to the nodes where NodeStatus.Allocatable is 0 and allowing Kubelet to admit them. This allows DRA to process such workloads.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
NONE
```

title: When kubelet restarts, admission still rejects pods
body:
### What happened?

When kubelet restarts, the previously running pod is rejected by admission. This https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/118635  fails to cover all scenarios.

```bash
`2025-07-31 16:58:54 - Pod|1000000-vp2qd - UnexpectedAdmissionError, Allocate failed due to no healthy devices present; cannot allocate unhealthy devices rdma/hca_shared, which is unexpected`
```


Cause:


```json
"containerStatuses": [
    {
      "name": "app",
      "state": {
        "running": {
          "startedAt": "2025-07-30T04:12:07Z"
        }
      },
      "lastState": {
        "terminated": {
          "exitCode": 0,
          "reason": "Completed",
          "startedAt": "2025-07-28T05:33:22Z",
          "finishedAt": "2025-07-30T04:09:41Z",
          "containerID": "containerd://491ae36456e71a83a6c39270e364e85306f583f959b386660262898086462374"
        }
      },
      "ready": true,
      "restartCount": 2,
      "image": "docker.io/ai/goglang:v0.0.1",
      "imageID": "docker.io/ai/goglang@sha256:be1692a1c0437b07c47a89417a33622b21a488f131520xxxxxxx",
      "containerID": "containerd://f393bcca6c8028c74f8987165759a472b3085f4bdf26173eb3dbb4cbe1f6cc9d",
      "started": true
    }
```

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/118635 use `isContainerAlreadyRunning` to check running container. It queries the id from the `containerMap`.

`containerMap` stores all containers on the nodes.(This includes exiting)

`containerMap` is a map, and when looking up the ID, it may return the exited container ID, not meeting expectations.

```shell
# nvida/gpu
I0731 16:58:54.195904  909172 manager.go:1100] "container found in the initial set, assumed running" podUID="58cf408f-5297-4209-96a0-f2c367392151" containerName="app" containerID="f393bcca6c8028c74f8987165759a472b3085f4bdf26173eb3dbb4cbe1f6cc9d"
I0731 16:58:54.195915 909172 manager.go:575] "container detected running, nothing to do" deviceNumber=0 resourceName="nvidia.com/gpu" podUID="58cf408f-5297-4209-96a0-f2c367392151" containerName="app"
# rdma
I0731 16:58:54.195953  909172 manager.go:1095] "container not present in the initial running set" podUID="58cf408f-5297-4209-96a0-f2c367392151" containerName="app" containerID="491ae36456e71a83a6c39270e364e85306f583f959b386660262898086462374"
I0731 16:58:54.196046 909172 manager.go:580] "Need devices to allocate for pod" deviceNumber=0 resourceName="rdma/hca_shared" podUID="58cf408f-5297-4209-96a0-f2c367392151" containerName="app"
```






### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet restart, pod still running.

title: Patching doesn't work with pods with annotation based app armor configuration in Kubernets version 1.32
body:
### What happened?

Patching doesn't work with pods with ONLY annotation based app armor configuration in Kubernets version 1.32

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect the patch to go through

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This could be an issue before 1.32, but I only tested in 1.32.

If we have a pod that is still using the annotation based app armor profile (without the `appArmorProfile` field under `securityContext`), for example
```
 container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/container: localhost/<profile-name>
```

and we run a simple kubectl patch command
```
kubectl patch pod test-pod \
-p '[{"op": "remove", "path": "/metadata/labels/label"}]' \
--type=json
```

The request will fail with message (only showing the relevant part)
```
- 				AppArmorProfile: &core.AppArmorProfile{Type: "Localhost", LocalhostProfile: &"<profile-name>"},
+ 				AppArmorProfile: nil,
  			},
```
as if my patch is trying to remove the apparmor profile.

### Anything else we need to know?

I have tried patching the pod / deployment to onboard with the new apparmor profile. The edit went through but the resource didn't actually get updated with the appArmorProfile

I suspect that this behavior has something to do the mechanism where we are syncing the deprecated annotation to the `appArmorProfile` field under `securityContext`, probably it's not doing this when we are doing patches?

I believe the problem comes from how patching works with the new `securityContext.appArmorProfile` field  introduced in recent Kubernetes versions. What seems to be happening in 1.32 is that,  pod still uses the old annotation form for AppArmor so when we run `kubectl patch` to change something else, Kubernetes rebuilds the Pod spec internally using the new `securityContext.appArmorProfile` field. There is no step to copy the AppArmor value from the old annotation into the new field before calculating the diff, resulting in the Pod's internal version appearing to have no AppArmor profile. The diff logic treats this as a request to remove it.  In short, the backwards-compatibility logic that maps annotations to  `securityContext.appArmorProfile` is missing in the patch conversion flow

title: After getting UserNamespaces configured and setting idsPerPod, the uid/gid maps inside containers are not seeing the settings propagate
body:
### What happened?

Now that I have the UserNamespaces working thanks to the documentation updates in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132966, I have reconfigured my kubelet on each node to have `idsPerPod: 1048576`. However containers are not seeing the change and are limited to `65536` ids in their maps.

The process followed was:

* Edit the kubelet-configmap in kube-system to add the following:
```
userNamespaces:
  idsPerPod: 1048576
```

* Run `sudo kubeadm upgrade node phase kubelet-config`
* Run `systemctl restart kubelet`
* Check that the setting has propagated to each node:
```
kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/green02/proxy/configz" | yq -p json -o yaml | grep idsPerPod

    idsPerPod: 1048576

```

However when I hop into a usernamespaced pod on a kubelet with this config - I see the following:

```shell
cat /proc/self/uid_map
          0    5898240      65536 
```

So I can see the UID is remapped, but there's only 65536 assigned to the pod, even after deleting it an having it recreated. I'm missing something here and I do not see the answers I need in docs.

Open questions:
1. How does this propagate to the containers? Should I automatically see the new value in column 3 of the uid_map?
2. I notice the docs state that this id setting is _per pod_ - so what is the implication of ids per container in a multi container pod? Do I need to multiply up for that? Or is the limit in fact _per container_ and the naming here is misleading?
3. What is missing from the document here to get the e2e configuration working for a pod?

Details:
* `kubeadm`, `kubectl`, `kubelet` and `cri-o` at version `1.33.2`
* Baremetal hosts are Debian 12 running backport kernel `6.12.32-1~bpo12+1 (2025-06-21) x86_64`


Context:
I am trying to run a buildkit container in a UserNamespace, and it cannot write to the `uid_map` - After trying `procMount: Unmasked`, ensuring the container is unconfined, and even marking it privileged the process keeps failing to start with `newuidmap: write to uid_map failed: Operation not permitted` and all evidence is pointing to the id allotment to the usernamespace being too small.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected that the `uid_map` and `gid_map` in the `/proc` mount of the containers would have an allocation of `1048576` ids.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

* Install Debian 12
* Install Kernel 6.12.* from backports to bring in supported features needed for this added in kernel 6.3
* Install crio, kubeadm, kubelet and kubectl version 1.33.2 as per the kubeadm cluster creation docs
* Install `uidmap` package via apt
* Configure kubelet user for submapping: `sudo adduser --system --no-create-home --disabled-login --group kubelet kubelet`
* Add following line to both `/etc/subgid` and `/etc/subuid` as per documentation: `kubelet:65536:7208960`
* Restart kubelet or restart node
* Edit the `kubelet-config` in `kube-system` and add:
    ```
    userNamespaces:
      idsPerPod: 1048576
    ```
* Run `sudo kubeadm upgrade node phase kubelet-config`
* Run `systemctl restart kubelet`
* Check that the setting has propagated to each node:
    ```
    kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/green02/proxy/configz" | yq -p json -o yaml | grep idsPerPod
    
        idsPerPod: 1048576
    
    ```
* Create a simple pod with `hostUsers: false`
    ```yaml
    ---
    kind: Pod
    apiVersion: v1
    metadata:
      name: admin-pod
    spec:
      hostUsers: false
      containers:
        - name: test
          image: debian:12
          # Write to a file inside our NFS
          command: ["sleep", "999999"]
    
    ```
* Check the resulting `uid_map` and `gid_map`:
    ```shell
    routhinator@routhinator-desktop [06:21:25] [~/projects/routh-forgejo/routh-ca/cluster-config/util] [main *]
    -> % kubectl exec -it admin-pod -- cat /proc/self/uid_map    (⎈|kubernetes-admin@red-squadron:default) 
             0    4849664      65536
    
    routhinator@routhinator-desktop [06:22:09] [~/projects/routh-forgejo/routh-ca/cluster-config/util] [main *]
    -> % kubectl exec -it admin-pod -- cat /proc/self/gid_map    (⎈|kubernetes-admin@red-squadron:default) 
             0    4849664      65536
    ```

### Anything else we need to know?

nodes.title: [Carry 133278] kubelet: Don't ignore idsPerPod config #133278
nodes.body:
Carry #133278, so as to address my own comments ([tests/e2e_node: Add test for userNamespaces.idsPerPod](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/133373/commits/53c35b747cb9e56fdb2cd4d8e20ee428394c00e6))

- - -
(Below is copied from #133278)

The idsPerPod where completely ignored since they were introduced in PR: #130028

The problem was the following:
1. The userns manager (as well as all managers) is created before the config is copied to the kubelet object[1](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/461ba83084ab7cb91ab692687bb7aedb05c6eb65/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L1078-L1087)
2. The userns manager on creation is calling the kubelet_getter GetUserNamespacesIDsPerPod to get the idsPerPod
3. The getter checks the configuration stored in the kubelet object, which hasn't been set at that point.
4. As the config ss nil (unset), it returns the default value.

Therefore, the value was ignored.

To solve this, let's just pass the idsPerPod as a parameter to MakeUserNsManager(). This is the common pattern already used in the kubelet initialization.

cc @AkihiroSuda @giuseppe

#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
We now honor the idsPerPod config from the kubelet.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
Fixes: #133144

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
The kubelet now honors the configuration userNamespaces.idsPerPod. Before it was ignored.
```

body:
### What happened?

Current private image pull e2e tests for kubelet rely on hardcoded credentials to a public repo that is getting decommissioned as a part of https://github.com/kubernetes/k8s.io/issues/1469. These tests will permafail once that happens.

### What did you expect to happen?

@BenTheElder what is the timeline for this? Is it absolutely critical for 1.33 or we can do it later?

TLDR: no

---


> @BenTheElder what is the timeline for this?

We are not setting any timeline ourselves, but the existing usage is an unfunded liability.

SIG K8s Infra is not going to repeat this on community infra with having a hardcoded service account baked into the tests that must remain valid for a publicly reachable SaaS endpoint (!), this is not sustainable to guarantee. It's amazing it has worked this long.

Nobody at Google is staffing this either, and the existing endpoints are not owned by SIG K8s Infra.

I don't currently have direct control over these, and nobody has responded to previously raising this repeatedly, while it only impacts a handful of tests for pulling private images, so I haven't been planning to do anything further either way.

> Is it absolutely critical for 1.33 or we can do it later?

It's not tied to 1.33, though GCR turndown is ~now, and we have to hope somebody went in and migrated this to AR to keep it functional for now (and hope the GCR enabled service account still continues to work).

My previous suggestion was an in-cluster registry, deployed by the tests, with some trivial image (pause?) and fixed credentials  pre-populated. 

The details may be tricky for portability though, it might have to be hostPort on a particular node or something like that to guarantee reachability by the runtime.

Not that cri-proxy would be less tricky to deploy portably.

It's possible to check if migrated, but we'll have to dig up the specific registries, and like everyone else code freeze is busy.

I outlined one way to check here: https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/issues/15199#issuecomment-2637803054

But either way:
- **This can likely wait another release or two or five**
- **This is bound to break eventually, probably without notice**, and when it does we're not going to copy-paste the unsupportable approach, so if anyone is invested in private image pull functionality, finding a better alternative ahead of time would be a good plan

/remove-priority important-soon
/priority important-longterm

This is currently slated to break in two weeks, I've requested an extension but we have to stop depending on this.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132882 seemed closely related.
FYI @kubernetes/sig-node-bugs

ok, one week is left... 

/remove-priority important-longterm
/priority important-soon
I don't think we will be able to fix it today before code freeze. But maybe we will be able to get exception for test-only update next week

This test: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e_node/runtime_conformance_test.go#L53 should be easy to switch to use cri proxy instead of the "real" registry.

This test https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e/common/node/runtime.go#L286 cannot be tested with the cri proxy. We can either try to create a "real" registry on the fly. Alternatively maybe we can fake the registry by deploying some host network enabled DaemonSet that will expose the registry endpoint on some localhost port. I wonder wht you think @BenTheElder on using this approach for cluster tests?
Another thing - we may limit tests to e2e_node-only. Since tests in common are not marked as conformance, we can remove them.

I'll take this 👍 Intuitively the private registry approach sounds more understandable to me, but I'll consider cri proxy as well, as it might be easier to implement (especially given that we don't need to keep tests in `common/node` and need to fix only conformance tests)

> Alternatively maybe we can fake the registry by deploying some host network enabled DaemonSet that will expose the registry endpoint on some localhost port. I wonder wht you think @BenTheElder on using this approach for cluster tests?

I think this is the most plausible approach for cluster e2e tests.

Someday maybe https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132955

> Another thing - we may limit tests to e2e_node-only. Since tests in common are not marked as conformance, we can remove them.

I think this is the most pragmatic approach, we have a lot more flexibility to sort out kubelet / cri <> registry communication in e2e_node, and I think the value of a cluster e2e for this codepath is kind of low as long as we have node_e2e.

> Alternatively maybe we can fake the registry by deploying some host network enabled DaemonSet that will expose the registry endpoint on some localhost port. I wonder wht you think @BenTheElder on using this approach for cluster tests?

the main problem is having a daemonset that is also a private registry, I can think of two approaches:

1. actually run the registry on every host, with some image available, and the auth configured
2. run the registry once, run a proxy daemonset on every host just to expose it as a hostport to the CRI reliably

there's also a third approach where instead of a proxy daemonset you use a clusterIP service but that's harder to make portable ...

We could possibly locally, in-cluster run something like the [CNCF distribution registry](https://distribution.github.io/distribution/). It seems to be quite easy to deploy and takes the [good old htpasswd ](https://distribution.github.io/distribution/about/deploying/#native-basic-auth) as an input for authn config.
I'm not sure which networks are available to the nodes, service network would be the easiest but I guess if that's not an option, having the service exposed via HostIP might be somewhat ok?

The registry would have to be fed some images somehow, too. I haven't done much around actually working with the OCI artifacts, but I guess the simplest thing would be to just do a couple HTTP calls as described in https://docs.docker.com/reference/api/registry/latest/#tag/pull (replacing docker specifics with standard OCI).
Perhaps something like https://github.com/containers/oci-fetch/tree/master, but simpler, more single-purpose built.
/cc @aramase @enj

> We could possibly locally, in-cluster run something like the [CNCF distribution registry](https://distribution.github.io/distribution/). It seems to be quite easy to deploy and takes the [good old htpasswd ](https://distribution.github.io/distribution/about/deploying/#native-basic-auth)as an input for authn config.


If possible we should look at integrating something minimal into agnhost instead.

We currently:
- only use images we host ourselves on registry.k8s.io
- are whittling down the set of images https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/131893 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/hack/verify-e2e-images.sh

This impacts a couple things:
1. being able to mirror images and test airgapped
2. insulating the project from third party registry pull quotas, downtime
3. being able to keep images patched (the images we re-hosted like redis are wildly out of date and nobody has the time to keep after dozens of random e2e images)

The registry API is pretty simple, and we only need one test image, I bet we could hack up something much tinier than a real registry.

See for example https://github.com/kubernetes/registry.k8s.io/tree/main/cmd/archeio


> I'm not sure which networks are available to the nodes, service network would be the easiest but I guess if that's not an option, having the service exposed via HostIP might be somewhat ok?

See the comments above about clusterIP or proxy daemonset.

> Perhaps something like https://github.com/containers/oci-fetch/tree/master, but simpler, more single-purpose built.

Throughout the project we have leveraged https://github.com/google/go-containerregistry (in sig-release and k8s-infra) AKA `crane` and the associated library, so we should probably use that again for OCI client code if needed.

https://cs.k8s.io/?q=go-containerregistry&i=nope&literal=nope&files=&excludeFiles=&repos=

@SergeyKanzhelev's  suggestion of cri-proxy in an e2e_node also seems like it might be a lot simpler, if we can just fake the CRI responses and avoid image networking altogether, we can still test the kubelet codepath and even kubelet <> api-server secrets.

We won't be testing credential plugins that way, but those are going to be vendor specific anyhow ... and the real incluster registry wouldn't either.

> The registry API is pretty simple, and we only need one test image, I bet we could hack up something much tinier than a real registry.

I guess, if necessary, building an HTTP server-image registry that responds to a couple requests shouldn't be too bad, true 👍

I am not that familiar with cri-proxy and what its capabilities are, but if it can mock CRI responses reasonably, perhaps that would be a way to go.
Credential plugins aside, I will have to implement e2e tests for the other new KEP https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2535 for the next Kube release, hopefully whatever we choose will still be compatible with it 🙂

But if we need to do something quick now and then move to whatever else seems reasonable, that is fine, too.

I thought that we can utilize criproxy to intercept `PullImage` command, check for a proper auth inside and then change the pulling url to the public one, without authorization (perhaps registry.k8s.io?). The objective of the conformance test is **"should be able to pull from private registry with credential provider"**, this way we can confirm this, right?

However, here are few things:
1. Currently, `criproxy` only can inject errors in the execution, not override the request or response. The behaviour injecting through `injectors` and they have only API method name in the signature right now, however it's probably should be easy to make them to act as a middlewares (modifying requests and responses). The point of interests are:
proxy runtime: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e_node/criproxy/proxy_runtime_service.go
image service: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e_node/criproxy/proxy_image_service.go

2. From a long term perspective (to test different behaviour when interacting with CRI), is this method looks like sufficient enough to test different behaviours of CRI, or you feel we need something more fulfilling, like our registry we spin up during test runs, or some mock server which replicate methods of the image registry?

> The objective of the conformance test is "should be able to pull from private registry with credential provider", this way we can confirm this, right?

A conformance test can't rely on cri-proxy, but a node_e2e could, and this probably isn't the most critical conformance test.

For a conformance test we will want to actually pull an image in a portable way, something like provisioning a clusterIP => pointing it at an in-cluster registry (@danwinship to confirm if that's reasonable from a SIG Net POV for conformance).

> I guess, if necessary, building an HTTP server-image registry that responds to a couple requests shouldn't be too bad, true 👍

Yeah, and serving up the most trivial image possible ... something like pause? We could store a copy in the test image.

> > I guess, if necessary, building an HTTP server-image registry that responds to a couple requests shouldn't be too bad, true 👍
> 
> Yeah, and serving up the most trivial image possible ... something like pause? We could store a copy in the test image.

it may be even small enough to include into agnhost.

> it may be even small enough to include into agnhost.

Er +1, that's what I intended to say by "store a copy in the test image".

On linux the pause image is less than a megabyte per architecture:

```console
$ for arch in amd64 arm64 ppc64le s390x; do crane export --platform=linux/$arch registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10.1 - | tar -xzf - --to-stdout | wc -c; done
  735760
  514000
  796712
  553416
```

Thank you for all your discussions, guys. That's very valuable feedback, and with all that being said, I believe the best option would be:
1. Implement the lightweight server which serves only one endpoint for pull images and have only one image - `pause` for all required platforms. The server should support base auth (with combination of user:password stored as a base64 in the auths part of config.json), so we would be able to use with the tests, which requires private registry (where we're using GCR right now)
2. Add this functionality to [agnhost](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/kubernetes/test/images/agnhost)? If I understand correctly what you're thinking about - we want to extend agnhost and add there something similar to [fake-gitserver](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/kubernetes/test/images/agnhost#readme-fake-gitserver) command?
3. In tests we start the agnhost with this command as a pod or daemonset with hostport (this part is unclear right now, as we have quite a few options here with different configurations, but probably can be discussed later)

If this sounds good, than I see two PR here - extend agnhost with the new command and fake registry inside (that means the new version of app, new images and all that) and a second - fix our tests which using the private registry right now.

P. S. I'm very new in the K8s project, sorry if some of my assumptions are not clear or off point.

> something like provisioning a clusterIP => pointing it at an in-cluster registry (@danwinship to confirm if that's reasonable from a SIG Net POV for conformance).

I'm not sure if conformance currently ends up requiring that hostNetwork processes can reach ClusterIP services, but it probably should...

From a portability perspective, this wouldn't work as a _general_ solution (e.g., if you need to pull the kube-proxy images off the ClusterIP-based registry), but that problem doesn't affect the e2e case where the cluster is already up and running before you set up the private registry.

title: Kubelet should not add IPv6 entries to /etc/hosts on systems where IPv6 is disabled
body:
### What happened?

Kubelet unconditionally adds IPv6 entries to `/etc/hosts` even when system has IPv6 totally disabled. This results in strange errors due to "happy eyeballs" fallback behavior: when clients see both an IPv4 and an IPv6 address for a host, they first try IPv4 and then fall back to IPv6, but if IPv6 is disabled in the kernel, they then get an "Address family not supported by protocol" exception instead of "Connection refused".

This happens with standard HTTP clients, etc, but here's an example with netcat:
```
# nc -v 127.0.0.1 1111
Ncat: Version 7.92 ( https://nmap.org/ncat )
Ncat: Connection refused.
```
vs
```
Ncat: Version 7.92 ( https://nmap.org/ncat )
Ncat: Connection to 127.0.0.1 failed: Connection refused.
Ncat: Trying next address...
libnsock nsock_make_socket(): Socket trouble: Address family not supported by protocol
Ncat: Address family not supported by protocol.
```

That results in clients needing to handle a different exception. However, even if IPv6 were enabled on the system, it would still be invalid to put loopback addresses in `/etc/hosts` for localhost when they are not actually configured on the loopback interface.

Code here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.29.4/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L373-L377

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should not add localhost entries to `/etc/hosts` for addresses that do not actually exist on the pod's loopback interface.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I don't think you need a reproducer for this one since the code is just unconditionally doing this. However, if you're looking to test this on a system with ipv6 disabled such that you get the "Address family not supported by protocol" error, or guarantee that CNI does not add an IPv6 loopback address, you can boot your kernel with `ipv6.disable=1` on the kernel command line.

### Anything else we need to know?
